paragraphs: Comparisons of models for tabular data often give every model a highly standardized preprocessing pipeline. This paper asks whether those comparisons reflect practical modeling, where people tailor data preparation and features to each dataset. Its central concern is that an evaluation can emphasize model choice while understating the contribution of the data pipeline.

The authors build an evaluation framework around ten Kaggle competition datasets, each with expert preprocessing. They vary preprocessing and hyperparameter optimization to examine the contributions of model selection, feature engineering, tuning, and adaptation at test time. This makes the overall modeling process part of the comparison.

After dataset-specific feature engineering, model rankings change substantially and performance gaps narrow. Both tree models and neural networks still benefit significantly from manual feature engineering. The study also finds that apparently static datasets can contain temporal distribution changes, making adaptation relevant. These results support evaluating tabular models together with realistic data preparation and temporal behavior, rather than treating preprocessing as a settled background choice.
neurips-2024-a-data-centric-perspective-.tldr: Realistic feature engineering changes tabular model rankings and narrows performance gaps, highlighting the importance of evaluating complete data pipelines.

paragraphs: This paper studies optimization across a network of agents that have no central server. Together, the agents minimize a sum of smooth, strongly convex functions. Existing methods often need global information about the functions or network connectivity to choose their settings. Individual agents may lack that information, making their choices overly cautious or unstable.

The proposed algorithm combines operator splitting with a new variable metric. Its practical feature is a local backtracking line search: agents adapt their step sizes without needing global parameter values or extensive communication. The method therefore addresses the difficulty of choosing suitable update sizes within a decentralized system.

For smooth, strongly convex objectives, the authors establish linear convergence, meaning that the optimization error decreases geometrically. They describe this as the first adaptive decentralized algorithm with that guarantee and report favorable dependence on problem and network parameters compared with nonadaptive methods. Preliminary numerical experiments support the theory through improvements in convergence speed and scalability; the formal claim remains tied to the stated objective class.
neurips-2024-achieving-linear-convergenc.tldr: A decentralized optimizer adapts step sizes using local information while achieving linear convergence for smooth, strongly convex objectives.

paragraphs: Computerized adaptive testing selects questions in response to a student's answers, aiming to estimate ability with relatively few questions. This paper focuses on a different consequence of testing: whether the resulting ordering of students matches their underlying abilities. Accurate individual estimates matter, but the authors argue that ranking deserves explicit attention in settings such as selective examinations.

The proposed Collaborative Computerized Adaptive Testing framework uses information across students. Conventional testing treats each student's assessment independently; CCAT instead uses collaborative students as anchors when ranking a test-taker. These anchors provide reference points for the relative comparisons that the final ordering requires.

The paper supplies theoretical guarantees and experimental validation for ranking consistency. Its contribution is therefore both a change in evaluation emphasis and a collaborative mechanism for pursuing that objective. By bringing relationships between students into the testing process, the method directly addresses the quality of the resulting ranking, rather than relying solely on the accuracy of separately estimated ability scores.
neurips-2024-computerized-adaptive-testi.tldr: CCAT uses other students as reference anchors to improve the consistency between adaptive-test rankings and underlying student abilities.

paragraphs: A language model can receive contextual information and still produce a statement that misreads it or has no grounding in it. This paper asks which parts of the supplied context actually led the model to generate a particular statement. It names this problem context attribution, making the relationship between a response and its input the object of investigation.

ContextCite is presented as a simple, scalable method for that task, applicable on top of any existing language model. The goal is to identify the relevant pieces of context, if there are any. This qualification matters: the problem includes statements for which an attribution to the supplied material may be absent.

The authors demonstrate three applications: helping verify generated statements, improving responses by pruning context, and detecting poisoning attacks. Together, these applications connect attribution to both inspecting outputs and changing the information a model receives. The stated contribution is a way to investigate contextual influence that supports these uses, rather than a claim that every attributed statement is necessarily correct.
neurips-2024-contextcite-attributing-mod.tldr: ContextCite identifies which parts of a model's context led to particular generated statements, supporting verification, context pruning, and poisoning detection.

paragraphs: Self-supervised vision models can predict responses of object-selective neurons as well as, or better than, models trained on labeled object recognition. Their lack of dependence on large labeled datasets also makes self-supervision an arguably more biologically plausible learning principle. This paper examines whether typical self-supervised objectives discard too much information about changes to an input.

The authors propose transforming standard invariant losses into contrastive-equivariant versions. Invariance encourages representations to remain unchanged under input transformations. The new framework instead encourages structured variation that preserves aspects of those transformations, without supervised access to their parameters. It retains information about how an input changes while still using self-supervised learning.

The method systematically improves the models' ability to predict responses in macaque inferior temporal cortex. The authors also report better alignment with known features of perception and neural computation. These findings support incorporating structured sensitivity to transformations into models of visual cortex, showing that stronger invariance is not always the most useful objective for predicting neural responses.
neurips-2024-contrastive-equivariant-sel.tldr: Preserving structured responses to image transformations improves self-supervised models' predictions of neural activity in macaque inferior temporal cortex.

paragraphs: Imitation learning trains an agent from expert demonstrations without requiring rewards from the environment. In generative adversarial imitation learning, a policy tries to resemble the expert while a discriminator learns to distinguish expert behavior from the agent's trajectories. This competition provides a learning signal, but its training can be brittle and unstable.

DRAIL introduces a diffusion model into that adversarial setup. The authors construct a diffusion-based discriminative classifier and use its outputs to define the rewards that train the policy. The intended benefit is a reward signal that is smoother and more robust, addressing the quality of the feedback available during imitation.

Experiments in navigation, manipulation, and locomotion demonstrate effectiveness relative to prior imitation learning methods. Additional experiments support generalizability and data efficiency. Visualizations of learned reward functions suggest that DRAIL can produce smoother, more robust rewards than GAIL. That visual evidence supports the proposed mechanism, while the task evaluations provide evidence that the modified reward construction helps agents learn from demonstrations.
neurips-2024-diffusion-reward-adversaria.tldr: DRAIL uses a diffusion-based discriminator to supply imitation-learning rewards, with experiments supporting effectiveness, generalizability, and data efficiency.

paragraphs: Exploration in reinforcement learning often uses uncertainty or entropy to encourage agents to visit unfamiliar situations. This paper argues that such approaches can overlook structure within the available states and actions. SI2E aims to make exploration sensitive to that structure, so that an agent's incentive reflects more than uncertainty about individual variables.

The method introduces structural mutual information and an embedding principle for representations relevant to the environment's dynamics. It examines value differences between state-action pairs and minimizes structural entropy to organize them into a hierarchy called an encoding tree. Within that hierarchy, it maximizes value-conditional structural entropy to construct an intrinsic reward that discourages redundant transitions and encourages broader coverage.

The authors establish theoretical connections to classical information-theoretic approaches and evaluate SI2E on MiniGrid, MetaWorld, and DeepMind Control Suite. They report significant improvements over state-of-the-art exploration baselines in final performance and sample efficiency, with maximum gains of 37.63% and 60.25%, respectively. These are maximum reported improvements, supporting the usefulness of structured exploration in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2024-effective-exploration-based.tldr: SI2E organizes state-action pairs into a hierarchy and uses structural entropy to reward exploration, improving performance and sample efficiency in reported benchmarks.

paragraphs: FinBen evaluates language models across a broad range of financial work. It contains 42 datasets covering 24 tasks, spanning information extraction, textual analysis, question answering, generation, risk management, forecasting, decision-making, and English-Spanish evaluation. The breadth is intended to address the difficulty of assessing financial capabilities through a narrow set of tasks.

The benchmark includes stock-trading evaluation, agent and retrieval-augmented generation evaluation, and two new datasets concerning regulations and stock trading. The authors evaluate 21 representative language models. This setup allows strengths in relatively focused text tasks to be considered alongside performance on more complex financial activities.

The evaluated models perform well on extraction and textual analysis but struggle with advanced reasoning, generation, and forecasting. GPT-4 leads in extraction and trading, while Gemini performs better in generation and forecasting. Instruction tuning helps textual analysis but gives limited benefits for complex tasks such as question answering. A shared task attracted 12 teams whose solutions outperformed GPT-4, illustrating the benchmark's usefulness for developing and comparing specialized approaches.
neurips-2024-finben-a-holistic-financial.tldr: FinBen evaluates financial language-model capabilities across 24 tasks, revealing strong text extraction but persistent difficulty with more complex work.

paragraphs: A standard graph neural network passes information along one graph. This paper considers several graphs sharing the same vertices and a common prediction task at those vertices. The resulting graph-tuple neural networks use multiple graph operators whose order can matter: applying one operator and then another need not produce the same result as reversing them.

The authors develop a mathematical account of stability and transferability using non-commuting, non-expansive operators. They also build a limiting framework based on graphon tuples. This provides a way to analyze how these networks behave across sequences of changing graphs, rather than considering only a single fixed graph collection.

Their universal transferability theorem applies to all graph-tuple neural networks on graph-tuple sequences converging in the specified sense. Under that convergence, no non-transferable energy remains. The results extend existing single-graph theory and improve it even in that setting. Synthetic and real-world experiments illustrate the theory, and a derived training procedure provably enforces model stability. The transfer guarantee depends on the paper's particular convergence framework.
neurips-2024-graph-neural-networks-and-n.tldr: The paper establishes stability and conditional universal transferability results for neural networks operating on several graphs with shared vertices.

paragraphs: Neural ordinary differential equations describe a network's hidden state as evolving continuously according to learned derivatives. Traditional batch normalization was designed for discrete networks without this temporal dimension. The paper identifies that mismatch as a significant obstacle to applying batch normalization effectively within Neural ODE models.

The authors introduce temporal adaptive batch normalization, or TA-BN, as a continuous-time counterpart to ordinary batch normalization. It brings the temporal dimension into the normalization approach. Their empirical findings show that TA-BN supports stacking more layers within Neural ODEs and improves performance, connecting the normalization change to the ability to build more capable models.

In an architecture containing a single Neural ODE followed by a linear layer, TA-BN reaches 91.1% test accuracy on CIFAR-10 using 2.2 million parameters. The authors describe this as the first unmixed Neural ODE architecture to approach MobileNetV2-level parameter efficiency. Experiments on image classification and physical-system modeling also show advantages over the evaluated baselines, providing evidence across both visual and dynamical modeling tasks.
neurips-2024-improving-neural-ode-traini.tldr: TA-BN adapts batch normalization to continuous-time Neural ODEs, enabling deeper models and improving reported accuracy and parameter efficiency.

paragraphs: Success on a single document page does not establish that a vision-language model can understand a long document. MMLONGBENCH-DOC tests that broader ability using 1,082 expert-annotated questions drawn from 135 PDFs. The documents average 47.5 pages and 21,214 text tokens, requiring models to work with substantial amounts of material.

Answers depend on evidence from text, images, charts, tables, and page layout, located across different pages. Cross-page questions make up 33.7% of the benchmark, while 20.6% are deliberately unanswerable to probe potential hallucinations. The evaluation therefore includes finding and combining evidence as well as recognizing when the document does not support an answer.

Among 14 evaluated vision-language models, GPT-4o achieves the highest F1 score at 44.9%, followed by GPT-4V at 30.5%. The other 12 perform worse than their language-model counterparts receiving imperfect OCR text. These findings show that access to document images did not consistently translate into better long-document understanding in the evaluated models, motivating further work on this capability.
neurips-2024-mmlongbench-doc-benchmarkin.tldr: MMLONGBENCH-DOC exposes substantial weaknesses in long-document vision-language understanding through questions requiring varied and cross-page evidence.

paragraphs: Organoids serve as models of human organs and their functions, but manually quantifying them in microscopy images creates a bottleneck for high-throughput analysis. MultiOrg addresses the need for open data to develop automated detection methods. It also gives explicit attention to uncertainty in human annotations, which relatively few biomedical datasets attempt to quantify.

The dataset contains more than 400 high-resolution two-dimensional microscopy images and curated annotations for over 60,000 organoids. Its test data have three label sets, independently produced by two experts at distinct time points. These repeated annotations make variation in labeling available for study rather than representing the test set through only one annotation set.

The authors additionally provide an organoid-detection benchmark and package its best model as an interactive, easily installed Napari plugin. This connects the dataset and model comparison to a tool for organoid quantification. The contribution combines resources for evaluating detection with a practical route to using the resulting model, while preserving annotation uncertainty as part of the research problem.
neurips-2024-multiorg-a-multi-rater-orga.tldr: MultiOrg provides organoid microscopy data with repeated expert annotations, a detection benchmark, and an interactive Napari quantification plugin.

paragraphs: Safety alignment can be weakened by fine-tuning, even with only a few adversarially designed examples. This paper investigates that risk by examining how safety changes as model weights are perturbed. The authors report a recurring pattern across the popular open-source language models studied: a local region around aligned weights where random perturbations preserve the original safety level.

They call this region a safety basin. Outside it, safety becomes fully compromised with a sharp drop in the observed landscape. Capability behaves differently: performance is highest at the original weights and declines gradually as perturbations increase. This contrast motivates VISAGE, a metric that assesses fine-tuning safety by probing the surrounding safety landscape.

The landscape visualizations show fine-tuning moving models away from the safety basin. They also highlight the protective role of system prompts, with that protection transferring to perturbed variants inside the basin. These observations offer a geometric way to investigate alignment risks and explain why gradual changes in capability need not mirror changes in measured safety.
neurips-2024-navigating-the-safety-lands.tldr: Observed safety basins around aligned model weights motivate VISAGE, a metric for investigating how fine-tuning compromises safety.

paragraphs: Existing permanental-process models often restrict the kernels they can use or assume stationarity. Those choices constrain how much the modeled relationships can vary across the data. This paper seeks greater flexibility, especially for data whose patterns are nonstationary, while also reducing the computational burden of fitting the model.

The proposed approach uses a sparse spectral representation of nonstationary kernels. This relaxes restrictions on both kernel type and stationarity, and the authors report reducing computational complexity to a linear level. They also introduce a deep-kernel variant that stacks several spectral feature mappings hierarchically, increasing the model's capacity to represent complex patterns.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the approach's effectiveness, particularly when nonstationarity is pronounced. Ablation studies examine how different hyperparameters affect performance. The combined contribution is a modeling approach that expands the kinds of variation a permanental process can express while improving computational scaling, with the deeper variant providing an additional mechanism for capturing complex data structure.
neurips-2024-nonstationary-sparse-spectr.tldr: Sparse spectral representations make permanental processes more flexible for nonstationary data while reducing reported computational complexity to a linear level.

paragraphs: Anchoring is a training principle that can be used across neural-network architectures and has shown benefits for uncertainty estimation, calibration, and extrapolation. This paper examines its use as a general protocol for vision models. The authors study both training and inference, asking how the protocol affects generalization and safety.

Their analysis identifies a problem in anchored training that can increase the risk of learning undesirable shortcuts. Such shortcuts can limit generalization, so the benefits previously associated with anchoring do not remove the need to examine how it is trained. The authors introduce a revised anchored-training protocol with a simple regularizer designed to mitigate this issue.

They evaluate the approach across datasets and architectures with different scales and levels of complexity. The reported results show substantial gains in generalization and safety metrics compared with standard training. The contribution therefore includes both identifying a failure mode of anchored training and modifying the protocol to address it, with empirical evidence that the revised approach improves the evaluated outcomes.
neurips-2024-on-the-use-of-anchoring-for.tldr: A revised anchoring protocol uses a simple regularizer to mitigate shortcut learning and improve vision models' measured generalization and safety.

paragraphs: When training is outsourced, clients need ways to check that the requested computation was performed correctly. One approach relies on a trusted auditor repeating the training process. However, different GPU types can introduce numerical nondeterminism, preventing exact replication and making this optimistic verification approach non-robust.

The proposed method controls those differences by combining higher-precision training with rounding after intermediate computations. It records rounding decisions using an adaptive thresholding procedure. These components make the numerical path reproducible at the target precision, addressing a concrete obstacle to comparing an auditor's run with the original training.

Across NVIDIA A40, Titan XP, and RTX 2080 Ti GPUs, the authors achieve exact FP32 replication for both full training and fine-tuning of ResNet-50 and GPT-2. The models contain 23 million and 117 million parameters, respectively. They also report significantly lower storage and time costs than proof-based systems. The result supports replication-based verification across the tested hardware and models, within a scheme that assumes a trusted third-party auditor.
neurips-2024-optimistic-verifiable-train.tldr: Controlled precision and recorded rounding decisions enable exact training replication across three GPU types for auditor-based verification.

paragraphs: Self-supervised learning extracts representations from unlabeled data, but those representations can suffer dimensional collapse: a few directions dominate while others contribute little. In features, this restricts the information represented. In weight matrices, it corresponds to related, redundant filters that limit expressive power. The paper examines collapse throughout the encoder.

Prior work has primarily addressed collapse in the final representations. The authors question whether that is sufficient to protect hidden features and weight matrices as well. Their proposed remedy applies orthogonality regularization to convolutional and linear layers during pretraining, encouraging weight matrices to contain less redundant directions.

The method is intended to safeguard weights, hidden features, and representations together by acting across the encoder. Empirical evaluations show significant improvements for self-supervised methods across diverse benchmarks, with consistent gains in both convolutional and Transformer-based architectures. These findings support treating dimensional collapse as a concern throughout the learned network, with regularization of its weights providing a practical intervention beyond focusing only on output representations.
neurips-2024-preventing-dimensional-coll.tldr: Orthogonality regularization throughout the encoder mitigates dimensional collapse and consistently improves evaluated self-supervised CNN and Transformer models.

paragraphs: Graph prompt learning adapts pretrained graph models through lightweight prompts that help reformulate downstream tasks to resemble pretraining tasks. It is motivated by inefficiency and negative transfer in conventional pretraining followed by fine-tuning, particularly in complex and few-shot settings. This paper addresses the difficulty of comparing the growing collection of graph prompt approaches.

The benchmark brings together six pretraining methods and five graph prompt techniques, evaluated on fifteen datasets. It assesses performance, flexibility, and efficiency. The authors also provide ProG, an open-source library designed to make running these models and conducting objective comparisons easier, supporting practical evaluation and method selection.

A unified framework organizes graph prompting into two categories: prompts represented as graphs and prompts represented as tokens. This gives otherwise diverse methods a shared structure for comparison. The paper's main contribution is therefore evaluation infrastructure and conceptual organization, making graph prompt approaches easier to study together. The abstract does not identify a single winning technique; its emphasis is on enabling consistent, usable comparisons.
neurips-2024-prog-a-graph-prompt-learnin.tldr: ProG unifies graph prompt methods in a benchmark and library covering six pretraining methods, five prompting techniques, and fifteen datasets.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning asks which cost function could explain an expert's observed optimal behavior. This paper studies that question for discrete-time, discounted Markov decision processes with continuous states and actions. It first considers access to the entire expert policy, allowing a mathematical characterization of the possible cost functions.

Using occupation measures, linear duality, and complementary slackness, the authors express the inverse problem as an infinite-dimensional linear feasibility problem. They add a linear normalization constraint to avoid trivial solutions and ill-posedness. This step matters because explaining observed behavior requires a meaningful formulation of the admissible costs, rather than merely finding any formally compatible function.

The authors then combine linear function approximators with randomized scenario methods to obtain approximately optimal solutions with probabilistic feasibility guarantees. They analyze the sample complexity needed for a desired approximation accuracy. Finally, they address the more realistic setting of finitely many expert demonstrations plus access to a generative model, providing bounds on the error introduced by using samples.
neurips-2024-randomized-algorithms-and-p.tldr: The paper develops randomized methods and probabilistic error guarantees for inferring costs from optimal behavior in continuous state and action spaces.

paragraphs: Reducing a vision Transformer's theoretical computation does not necessarily reduce its latency on a phone. Local attention and pruning can introduce reshaping, transposition, and irregular memory access. On mobile hardware with limited bandwidth, those costs can outweigh the arithmetic savings and even make an optimized model slower than a vanilla ViT.

ECP-ViT addresses this through coordinated algorithm and system design. It uses a core-periphery principle inspired by brain functional networks to guide self-attention, with the aim of reducing computation in a hardware-friendly way. The authors identify data transformations as a central bottleneck and add system optimizations for the intensive transformations found in pruned models.

The combined framework achieves reported mobile-GPU speedups ranging from 4.6 to 26.9 times across STL-10, CIFAR100, TinyImageNet, and ImageNet. These results support the value of designing attention and data handling together. The broader practical finding is that deployment speed depends on how computation and data movement map to the device, so theoretical operation counts alone can misrepresent mobile performance.
neurips-2024-real-time-core-periphery-gu.tldr: ECP-ViT combines hardware-friendly attention and data-transformation optimizations to deliver reported mobile-GPU speedups of 4.6 to 26.9 times.

paragraphs: Graph autoencoders learn to reconstruct graphs and can use reconstruction error to identify unusual ones. A common approach averages errors across nodes or node pairs, treating a high mean as evidence of an anomaly. This relies on the expectation that graphs resembling the majority will be reconstructed more accurately.

The paper presents counterexamples to that expectation, calling the phenomenon reconstruction flip. The authors analyze theoretically and empirically when the assumption holds and when it fails. Their response preserves reconstruction errors as useful information while questioning whether a single average captures enough of that information for reliable graph-level anomaly detection.

MUSE represents each graph through multiple summaries of its reconstruction errors. These summaries provide a more varied description than the mean alone, allowing the detection method to use several aspects of reconstruction behavior. Across ten datasets and fourteen compared methods, MUSE performs best overall. The findings connect an identified weakness in a common anomaly score to a simple remedy that retains the underlying reconstruction-based approach.
neurips-2024-rethinking-reconstruction-b.tldr: MUSE improves graph anomaly detection by using multiple reconstruction-error summaries after showing that mean error can behave contrary to standard assumptions.

paragraphs: Diffusion generation commonly breaks a reverse denoising process into many numerical steps. This paper interprets those steps as sampling subproblems defined by reverse transition kernels. DDPM approximates each kernel with a Gaussian, making individual subproblems cheap but requiring many segments; the authors conjecture that this balance is inefficient.

Their framework changes the decomposition to obtain a number of subproblems that is constant up to suppressed logarithmic factors, each with a strongly log-concave target. They solve these subproblems using either the Metropolis-Adjusted Langevin Algorithm or Underdamped Langevin Dynamics, producing RTK-MALA and RTK-ULD. The approach trades the original decomposition for subproblems suited to these sampling algorithms.

The authors establish convergence guarantees measured in total variation distance. Under mild conditions, RTK-ULD reaches error epsilon with complexity scaling as the square root of dimension divided by epsilon, up to logarithmic factors. Under slightly stricter conditions, RTK-MALA has a dimension-squared times logarithmic rate. The paper reports that these bounds improve on prior state-of-the-art rates, with numerical experiments supporting the theoretical results.
neurips-2024-reverse-transition-kernel-a.tldr: A reverse-transition-kernel framework reorganizes diffusion sampling into strongly log-concave subproblems and yields improved convergence bounds under stated conditions.

paragraphs: Optimizing a safety-critical system becomes harder when both performance and safety conditions change over time. The decision-maker must improve an unknown reward while respecting unknown constraints that may also move. This paper addresses that setting, motivated by sequential decision problems such as robotics and process control.

TVSAFEOPT uses Bayesian optimization with a spatio-temporal kernel, incorporating both the decision variables and time into its model. It can safely track a changing safe region without a separate mechanism for explicitly detecting changes. The authors also provide optimality guarantees when the optimization problem becomes stationary, giving the method a stated guarantee for the case where the environment stops changing.

On synthetic data, TVSAFEOPT compares favorably with SAFEOPT in both safety and optimality. A realistic gas-compressor case study further demonstrates safe optimization with unknown, time-varying reward and constraint functions. These findings support explicitly modeling temporal change when choosing safe actions, while the optimality result has the specific condition that the problem eventually becomes stationary.
neurips-2024-safe-time-varying-optimizat.tldr: TVSAFEOPT tracks changing safe regions through spatio-temporal Bayesian optimization and provides optimality guarantees when the problem becomes stationary.

paragraphs: Comparing physiological time series across individuals can help describe variation in biological function. This paper develops an unsupervised representation method tailored to those comparisons. Its central idea is to describe each individual's time series by the deformation needed to relate it to a learned reference time series.

The method, TS-LDDMM, jointly learns the reference and parameterized deformations called diffeomorphisms. Each time series then receives a vector representation consisting of the parameters of its deformation. This connects representation learning to shape analysis: the representation expresses how the individual's temporal shape differs from the shared reference. The method accommodates multivariate series with irregular sampling and varying lengths.

The authors establish a representation theorem for the graph of a time series and examine its consequences for the LDDMM framework. They also demonstrate advantages over existing representations using synthetic data and real examples motivated by biomedical applications. The contribution combines a mathematical foundation with a way to encode inter-individual variation through learned changes in temporal shape.
neurips-2024-shape-analysis-for-time-ser.tldr: TS-LDDMM represents irregular, variable-length time series through learned deformations of a shared reference, supporting shape-based comparisons between individuals.

paragraphs: Pretrained language models can perform many tasks, but controlling their behavior remains difficult. Reinforcement learning from human feedback can improve instruction following and preference alignment, yet it may also harm reasoning or introduce fabricated content. This paper proposes a different way to incorporate preference signals into a language model.

Direct Preference Heads adds an auxiliary reward head that learns human preferences during fine-tuning. The framework is designed to do this without directly affecting the output distribution of the language-modeling head. Its central architectural choice gives preference learning its own head, allowing preference information to be represented separately from the head responsible for language-model outputs.

The authors analyze their objective and identify strong connections to Conservative Direct Preference Optimization. They then evaluate models on GLUE, RACE, and the GPT4All evaluation suite, reporting higher scores than models using supervised fine-tuning or Direct Preference Optimization alone. These findings support the framework as an effective preference-learning approach in the evaluated settings; the reported benchmark advantage does not itself establish that hallucinations are eliminated.
neurips-2024-would-i-lie-to-you-inferenc.tldr: Direct Preference Heads learns preferences through an auxiliary reward head and achieves higher reported evaluation scores than SFT or DPO alone.
